[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Locking Mechanics and Deadlock Troubleshooting in PostgreSQL"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"PostgreSQL provides robust concurrency control through various locking mechanisms. Understanding how locks operate and how to troubleshoot deadlocks is critical for maintaining high-performance database applications."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding PostgreSQL Lock Types"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"PostgreSQL uses several levels of locks to manage concurrent data access. These range from table-level locks to row-level locks."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Row-Level Locks: Automatically acquired during data modification (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE). They do not block reads."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Table-Level Locks: Managed automatically during schema changes or explicit LOCK table commands. Types include ACCESS SHARE, ROW SHARE, ROW EXCLUSIVE, and ACCESS EXCLUSIVE."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Advisory Locks: Application-defined locks managed entirely by the user for custom synchronization logic."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Identifying Current Locks"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"To diagnose blocking issues, you must inspect the pg_locks system view combined with pg_stat_activity to see which queries are holding or waiting for locks."},{"order":10,"type":"code","text":"SELECT
    pid,
    usename,
    pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocked_by,
    query AS current_statement
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0;"},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"What is a Deadlock?"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"A deadlock occurs when two or more transactions are mutually blocked, each waiting for a lock held by the other. PostgreSQL automatically detects deadlocks and aborts one of the transactions (the "deadlock victim") to allow the other to complete."},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"Troubleshooting and Preventing Deadlocks"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"When a deadlock occurs, PostgreSQL logs an error containing the transaction details. Inspecting the PostgreSQL server log is the primary way to diagnose the root cause."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Consistent Order: Always access tables and rows in the same order across different transactions and application threads."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Short Transactions: Keep transactions as short as possible to minimize the window of lock contention."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Appropriate Isolation Levels: Use Read Committed where possible, and carefully design application logic around Repeatable Read or Serializable isolation."},{"order":18,"type":"code","text":"-- Example of explicit row locking with NOWAIT to fail fast instead of deadlocking
BEGIN;
SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE NOWAIT;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;
COMMIT;"}]
